verdicts.why: A's mark doesn't survive one-color or reversed use: the M and river wave disappear and only a blank solid hexagon is left. Its thin wave line also turns to mush at 16 px. B's stacked Langstroth-hive mark comes from the client's own product, keeps the same shape at 16 and 32 px, and works in one ink and reversed. B's sturdy serif lockup also reads more deliberately than A's familiar hexagon-plus-initial badge.

B's one-color and reversed marks are just solid hexagons: the M and the river wave disappear, so the logo fails on caps, vinyl and burned frames. That outweighs its stronger Maumee-river idea. A's stacked hive-box mark is a simple solid shape that reads the same at 16 and 32 px and holds up in one ink and reversed. It draws on the client's own product, and the serif wordmark is set carefully, though the idea is plainer.

Both spell the name exactly and invent nothing, and both marks are just the initials O and R, so neither has a real idea. B wins on the brief's second test: its heavy, simple O and R stay the same clear shape at 32 and 16 px and in one color, while A's thin serif OR blurs inside the circle at 16 px, and its fine serifs and light subline are risky for cut vinyl. A's lockup is better balanced and its round mark suits the circle avatar. B's mark is too small next to the wordmark and its R counter nearly closes up, so the margin is slight.

Both spell the name correctly and add nothing to it. A's heavy geometric O and R stay the same clear shape at 32 and 16 px and are solid enough to cut in white vinyl. B's thin serif 'OR' blurs inside its circle at 16 px, and its light 'Certified Public Accountants' line in Cormorant would be fragile on the glass door. Neither idea comes from the client's own subject, since both are initial monograms, but A's bold, custom-looking letterforms are more distinctive than B's default serif in a circle, which any competitor could use as-is.

Both spell the name correctly and invent nothing. A falls apart in one color: the otter's head merges into the solid circle so only a muzzle and thin whiskers are left, and the thin whiskers and wave line turn to mush at 16 px. That rules it out for swim caps, signage and the app icon. B's solid otter head peeking over a waterline keeps the same shape at 16 px, one color and reversed. It could be mistaken for a bear or hippo, and the mark is undersized in the lockup, but it is a usable mark that holds up wherever the client needs it.

B's otter head is drawn only with brown and blue fills, so in the one-color and reversed versions it disappears into the circle and only a muzzle and wave line remain, which is useless for a one-color swim cap. Its thin whiskers and wave also turn to mush at 16 and 32 px. A's solid otter head above a waterline bar keeps the same recognizable shape at 16 px, in one ink and reversed, though its bare geometry makes it more generic and a little robot-like than B's friendlier but more cartoon-mascot otter.

B's system fits this client more closely. Its imagery rules are specific enough to judge a photo against (crews and poles along Rice County fence rows in daylight, members at kitchen tables or the Lyons counter, no fake golden-hour filters), and its voice examples come straight from brief facts. A's photo section has awkward headings (a PHOTOS label, then a separate DO list), its type statement wraps clumsily, and its stacked-section layout reads more like a template. B has two flaws: the 'Feed Sack on Signal' swatch shows light text on a light background instead of on the accent, and it redraws the wordmark rather than showing logo.svg. Neither paper puts invented facts on the page, so craft and fit to the client decide it.

Both pages stick to the facts in the brief, and both give hex values, color roles and contrast ratios. A's imagery rules are specific enough to judge a photo against (crews and poles along Rice County fence rows in daylight, members at kitchen tables or the Lyons counter, no faked golden-hour glow). B's photo 'DO' list is mostly about signed releases, not how the pictures should look. A's voice principles and Say/Not pairs sound more like this co-op, and its sizes, logo lockups and clear-space rules are laid out cleanly. B's type block reads awkwardly ('Fraunces / Headlines. Source Sans 3 for all other text.') and its seven-color palette is harder for volunteers to follow.

verdicts.why: Neither page invents facts. A gives each color a clear role: plum for identity, an ember accent for the single action per page, and sage for checks. Its three voice principles each come with a matched Do and Don't line that a writer could follow directly, and its imagery rules are specific. B adds useful logo rules and a sensible 18 px body size, but its palette is almost entirely plum with no distinct accent. Its logo section also contradicts itself: the one-color rule names Night Plum while the samples show Hearthstone Plum. Its long contrast table takes up space that could have gone to voice guidance. A's one flaw is that it shows a 15 px body sample after saying web body text is never under 18 px.

verdicts.why: A has no invented facts, has no internal contradictions, and gives the printer logo rules (clear space, minimum size, one-color use) and a full table of color roles and contrast ratios, which B leaves out entirely. But it says web body text is never under 18 px, then sets body copy at 15 px in its own type scale, and its crisis line promises a 24-hour plan the brief never mentions.

verdicts.why: B ties the system to this specific gym. Its voice lines read like a coach talking ("Open 5 a.m. before the shift"), its imagery rules refer to the dealership building, and it names both fonts, Oswald and Source Sans 3, with a full size scale. A is a cleaner, well-ordered page with a useful pass/fail contrast table, but it names only Barlow Condensed and leaves the body font unnamed, and it barely uses the brief's sense of place. B's faults are smaller craft and accuracy issues: the Iron Oxide contrast ratio conflicts with its own table (5.8:1 vs 5.07:1), one imagery bullet repeats another, and the logo tile on the rust background is tiny. It also assumes brick and showroom windows that the brief never mentions.

verdicts.why: B is the more complete and usable system. It names five colors with hex values and clear roles, and it lists contrast pairs that fail, so staff know what never to combine. Its voice section gives three rules, each with a Do and a Don't, including 'Strong at 20, strong at 60' for the over-50 class. It also covers logo misuse and Instagram format, all in a numbered layout with intent. B's 13 px body and 11 px captions run small for print, which keeps the margin slight.

verdicts.why: Both use the brief's dogs, services, prices and three days correctly. A labels every time with AM/PM, lists services as a clear radio list with prices, and keeps a summary bar ('Full groom for Biscuit · Tue, Nov 10 · 10:30 AM with Bree · $85') above the confirm button. Its error banner names the lost slot, says Biscuit and the Full groom are still selected, and strikes through the taken time. B fits all three days on screen and marks the lost slot as 'booked' more clearly, but its bare times ('1:00', '3:30') are ambiguous, and its wrapping service pills and title-plus-dog-picker repetition feel less resolved. A's Thursday row is cut off by the footer on the first screen.

Both use the brief's dogs, services, prices and groomers correctly, and both error states name the taken slot, strike it through in the grid and say Biscuit and Full groom are still selected. B is easier to use: its times carry AM/PM where A's bare '1:00' and '3:30' are ambiguous, its sticky summary keeps the booking and the $85 price in view on both screens, and its labelled sections, radio-list services and type system make it look like a finished product. A's advantage is that all three days fit on screen 1 and its time buttons are larger, but its pill-shaped services and plainer layout look more like a template.

verdicts.why: A's mark comes from this client's own subject: a honeycomb hexagon holding Maumee River waves and a honey drop. It keeps the same recognizable hexagon at 32 and 16 px, and it holds up in one ink and reversed, though the drop gets muddy at 16 px. B's nested bracket/E shape is very sharp at small sizes but has nothing to do with bees, honey, the river or the store's name, so any company could use it. Its wordmark is a default bold sans, which gives it the generic feel the brief penalizes. Both spell the name exactly and invent nothing, so the decision rests on the idea and the craft, and A wins both.

A holds up best at small sizes: its blocky E stays crisp at 16 px and in one color, while B's waves and honey drop blur into a striped hexagon at 16 px, and in one-ink the drop merges with the waves. But A's mark is an arbitrary E that doesn't match the name's initials and has nothing to do with bees, honey or the river, and the name is set in what looks like a default bold sans, so it reads as generic. B's hex cell, Maumee River waves and honey drop come from this client's own subject, and its serif lockup is more deliberate, so it's the one I would hand over, though its small-size and one-color versions need simplifying.

Both spell the name correctly and add no invented words. B's solid O with a cut-out R stays the same bold shape at 32 and 16 px and holds up in one color and reversed, which matters for the small circle profile picture and the vinyl door. A's thin nested arches and outline R turn into faint rings at 16 px and its hairline strokes are fragile. B's R is a little awkward and looks like a P with a notch, but A's finer drawing doesn't make up for losing the mark at small sizes.

Both spell the name correctly and add nothing the client didn't give. A's solid O with an R cut into it stays the same recognizable shape at 32 and 16 px and holds up as one color, reversed, and in white vinyl. B's thin nested arch and circle lines blur into grey at 16 px and would be fragile cut in vinyl. B's idea is also weaker: an arch around an R is a generic doorway motif that drops Okafor, while A's O and R monogram belongs to both partners, though A's 'Certified Public Accountants' line is set too small.

A's one-color and reversed versions break down: the eyes and face details disappear, leaving a cat-eared blob with a stray squiggle that would not survive printing on a one-color swim cap. Its mascot also looks more like a cat or pig than an otter. B's heavy, simple mark keeps the same shape at 16 and 32 px and reads cleanly in one color and reversed, but it is an unclear cat-like glyph in a default-looking bold sans, so it wins only on durability.

Both spell the name exactly and invent nothing. The main difference is survival: A is a bold, evenly weighted outline that keeps the same shape at 16 and 32 px and works in one ink and reversed. B's one-color version fills in to a solid blob that loses the eyes and face, its thin wave line breaks up at small sizes, and the full-color version is a cartoon mascot that looks babyish. A's mark is still odd and reads more like a cat than an otter, and its type is a near-default sans, so it doesn't win on idea or craft. It wins because it would actually hold up on the swim caps, the app icon and the building.

verdicts.why: A fills the page with a clear hierarchy and readable body text. Every color has a hex value and a stated role (ground, surface, ink, accent), and its SAY/AVOID pairs and photo do/don't lists are concrete enough to guide a volunteer or judge a photo. B has the warmer and more distinctive palette and type pairing, but it leaves the bottom third of the letter page empty. Its labels, contrast notes and photo rules are set very small, and its contrast note refers to a 'Cream' that doesn't match the swatch name 'Field Cream'. Those flaws matter more to a printer than B's stronger personality. A's main weaknesses are a generic look and two white swatches with the same #FFFFFF value.

Both pages stick to facts from the brief, but B is the more complete system to hand off. It gives each hex value a role, adds a contrast table that says what each pair is safe for, shows a named type scale in px, sets logo clear-space and color rules, and has four concrete imagery do's and don'ts. A is clean and its voice do/don't pairs are good, but it leaves roughly a fifth of the page empty, never covers how to use the logo, and its type sizes come with no units. B has small flaws: the footer lists 'logo.svg' twice, it shows a typeset wordmark instead of the supplied logo, and the wordmark on the sage tile is tiny.

verdicts.why: Neither page invents facts. Both use only the brief's details: 4 hours a week to around the clock, 38 background-checked caregivers, and training by Grace Mbeki, RN. A is the more complete tool for the printer and web person: it shows the wordmark on three backgrounds with a clear-space rule, gives every color a hex value and a role backed by a pairwise contrast table, and lists a six-step type scale. B never shows the logo, leaves the bottom fifth of the page empty, and only partly makes up for it with sharper voice examples and good imagery rules. A has small craft slips of its own: the footer says 'logo.svg, logo.svg', the contrast ratios on the swatches don't match the ones in the table, and it repeats Porcelain as a 'Porcelain on Sage' swatch.

B is the more complete working system. It shows the logo on light, dark and orange backgrounds with a clear-space rule, gives every color a hex value, a role and a use, includes a full contrast table, names the type with weights and a px scale, and has specific imagery do/don't rules (staged lifts, before-and-after shots, age stereotypes) that a photo can be checked against. A is clean and its voice examples are good, but it never shows the logo, its imagery guidance is one short paragraph, and the bottom third of the page is empty. B has small flaws (the footer lists 'logo.svg, logo.svg' twice and a long contrast table), but neither invents anything significant and B gives the printer, staff and web person far more to work from.
